analysis.one_liner: Has the Energy Department guarantee prices for coal power and captured carbon dioxide for up to 25 years.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2015 and given a single Senate Energy Committee hearing, the bill never reached a vote and expired when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Department of Energy sign 25-year, legally binding contracts to prop up prices for electricity generated from coal, or for the carbon dioxide that coal plants capture and sell — mainly to oil companies that inject CO2 into old wells to push out more crude. The stated goal was to make carbon-capture projects easier to finance, but the mechanism is a long-term federal price guarantee for coal power and CO2-for-oil. The bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and developers of coal-fired power plants, who would get a federal guarantee on the price of their electricity or of the CO2 they capture, making expensive carbon-capture projects financeable; and oil producers, who buy captured CO2 to recover more crude from aging fields and would no longer face the volatile CO2 prices that track crude oil prices.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would let the Energy Secretary sign binding federal contracts of up to 25 years providing price stabilization support for electricity from coal-based generating units or for CO2 captured from them, giving project developers a guaranteed revenue stream.

The bill's own findings say the market price for captured CO2 swings with crude oil prices, and that a guaranteed CO2 price would give debt providers and investors the certainty they need to finance carbon-capture projects on coal plants.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, who would stand behind the federal government's side of 25-year binding price-guarantee contracts; if prices fell short of the guaranteed level, the difference would come from the Treasury. To the extent the guarantees keep coal plants running that would otherwise close, the costs of prolonged coal generation fall on the public as well.

drawbacks.text: The price support can go to electricity from a coal plant even where no carbon is captured — the CRS summary describes stabilization for 'electricity generated at an electric generation unit (that uses coal-based generation technology),' so the bill functions in part as a plain coal-power price floor.

The captured CO2 would chiefly be sold for crude oil recovery, meaning the carbon captured from coal would be used to pump more oil out of the ground, undercutting the climate rationale for capturing it.
Contracts would be binding on the federal government for up to 25 years, so taxpayers would bear the cost for decades if market prices fell below the guaranteed levels.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Developing carbon capture on coal plants is a legitimate stated goal, but this design pays for it in the most expensive and least climate-effective way: a 25-year federal guarantee on coal power itself, and a CO2 market built on selling captured carbon to oil producers. Taxpayers absorb the downside if prices fall, while the climate benefit is diluted by the extra oil recovered. The bill never advanced far enough for these trade-offs to be tested, and it had minimal support — a sponsor and one cosponsor.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee held one hearing in May 2015 and never acted on the bill again, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Heidi Heitkamp introduced the bill on May 11, 2015; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
The committee held a hearing on May 19, 2015, with the hearings printed as S.Hrg. 114-118.
No markup, floor vote, or further action ever followed; the bill expired with the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers came out ahead: they were never locked into 25-year price guarantees for coal power and CO2-for-oil. Coal and oil interests lost nothing they already had — they simply never got the new federal price support.

for.name: Sen. Heidi Heitkamp
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK)
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing and never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by two Democrats and died in a Republican-chaired committee without ever getting a vote, so no voting pattern exists to judge partisanship.

industries.note: Federal price guarantees for electricity from coal-based units — capture or not — would lower the financing risk of new coal plants and extend the market for coal. The industry's gain would come from long-term federal commitments rather than from competitive prices.

industries.industry: Oil producers using CO2 injection (enhanced oil recovery)
industries.note: These producers buy captured CO2 to force more crude out of aging wells; a federally stabilized CO2 price would cut their input costs and shield them from oil-price swings. Their gain comes directly from the taxpayer-backed contract the bill creates.

The bill's stated purpose is to make carbon-capture equipment on coal plants financeable by guaranteeing the revenue from captured CO2, which would mean new business for firms that build and operate that equipment.
